title: A Scalable Pretraining Framework for Link Prediction with Efficient Adaptation

problem.claim: Link prediction is challenged by sparse supervision, sensitivity to initialization, and poor generalization under distribution shifts.

gap.claim: Pretraining for link prediction must integrate node- and edge-level information, and existing methods do not systematically address transferability across these modules or diversity in pretraining data.

contributions.claim: A late fusion strategy combines node-level and edge-level module outputs for link prediction.
A Mixture-of-Experts pretraining framework separates distinct patterns to support application across diverse downstream datasets and reduce negative transfer.
A parameter-efficient tuning strategy adapts pretrained models to unseen datasets with minimal computational overhead.

author_reported_evidence.claim: Experiments cover 16 datasets across two domains.
The approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on low-resource link prediction.
The approach obtains competitive results relative to end-to-end trained methods with over 10,000x lower computational overhead.

narrative_sequence.summary: Link prediction is an important graph machine learning task, but current methods face supervision, initialization, and distribution-shift challenges.
The work investigates pretraining to address these challenges while accounting for the pairwise nature of link prediction.
The approach studies module transferability, combines node- and edge-level outputs through late fusion, and uses MoE pretraining for diverse data.
Parameter-efficient tuning enables adaptation to unseen datasets with low computational overhead.
Experiments across 16 datasets and two domains report strong low-resource performance, competitive end-to-end comparisons, and substantially lower computational overhead.

source_observation.claim: Link prediction requires both node-level and edge-level information because it is a pairwise task.

interpretation.claim: Architectures for pairwise graph tasks may benefit from explicitly separating and recombining representations at different structural levels.

application.claim: When designing transfer-learning systems for pairwise graph prediction, evaluate module-level transferability and consider late fusion.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish whether late fusion is beneficial for tasks that are not pairwise or do not require both node- and edge-level information.

source_observation.claim: A Mixture-of-Experts framework is used to capture distinct patterns in diverse pretraining data and avoid negative transfer.

interpretation.claim: Separating heterogeneous patterns across experts may improve transfer across diverse downstream datasets.

application.claim: For pretraining across heterogeneous datasets, consider expert specialization together with parameter-efficient downstream adaptation.

exception.claim: The abstract does not specify when expert specialization fails or how its benefits vary across dataset types.

unknowns: The abstract does not identify the 16 datasets or the two domains.
The abstract does not describe baselines, evaluation metrics, or experimental settings.
The abstract does not provide the absolute performance values or define the computational-overhead measurement.
The abstract does not report ablations, adaptation details, or failure cases.
